title: Attribute usage across the logs
prompt: Before choosing which log attributes to index, the logging team wants to know how widely each one is used. Write `solve(application_logs_raw)` so it parses the raw lines and returns, for every attribute key, how many records carry it and how many different services those records come from.
rules: Only lines that are JSON objects count; skip the rest. A record whose `attributes` is missing, null, empty or not an object carries no keys.
`records` counts the records that carry the key; a record shipped twice counts twice.
`services` counts the different `service` values among those records. A record with no `service` adds to `records` but not to `services`.
Return `attribute` (text), `records` and `services` (both `bigint`), in that order. An empty file gives an empty result.
hints: Parse safely with `flatMap`, then use a second `flatMap` to turn each record into one pair per attribute key.
A value can hold a Python set: `(1, {service})`. Two sets combine with `|`, whatever the order.
After `reduceByKey`, `len()` of the set is the number of services. Leave a missing service out of the set.
explanation: Parse each line with a function that returns `[record]` or `[]`, then `flatMap` every record into `(key, (1, {service}))` pairs, one per attribute key, with an empty set when the service is missing and no pairs when `attributes` isn't a dict. `reduceByKey(lambda a, b: (a[0] + b[0], a[1] | b[1]))` adds the counts and unions the sets, which works in any order, and `len` of the set gives the services. Counting 1 per record for services counts records again, and `attributes or {}` would walk through a list's items as if they were keys.
